title: DOES GOD STOP BLESSING YOU WHEN YOU STOP TITHING? THE TRUTH ABOUT MONEY, MALACHI 3:10, AND THE GOD WHO CANNOT BE BOUGHT
paragraphs: DOES GOD STOP BLESSING YOU WHEN YOU STOP TITHING? THE TRUTH ABOUT MONEY, MALACHI 3:10, AND THE GOD WHO CANNOT BE BOUGHT

What if the blessing you are terrified of losing was never something your money could purchase? Before you give another offering out of fear—or stop giving because you've been wounded—there is something Jesus wants you to understand.
She stared at the offering envelope longer than she wanted to admit.
Inside her purse was just enough money for groceries, transportation, and a few bills already overdue.
Her child needed something for school. The electricity payment was approaching. And the little money she had managed to save was disappearing faster than she could earn it.
Then the preacher said something that made her stomach tighten.
“If you don't give God His ten percent, don't expect Him to bless the other ninety.”
She looked down.
Her fingers tightened around the envelope.
And suddenly, she wasn't thinking about worship anymore.
She was thinking about punishment.
What if I don't give?
What if God allows something terrible to happen?
What if this is why my prayers haven't been answered?
What if my family is struggling because I haven't been faithful enough?
So she gave.
Not because her heart overflowed with gratitude.
Not because she was overwhelmed by the goodness of Jesus.
But because she was afraid.
And walking home that afternoon, carrying the same financial burdens she had brought to church, she whispered a question she would never dare ask aloud.
“Lord, do You still love me when I cannot afford to give?”
Maybe you've never held that envelope.
But perhaps you've held that fear.
You've heard testimonies about people who tithed and received unexpected promotions, financial breakthroughs, new businesses, and miraculous provision.
And you've wondered why you kept giving but still lost your job.
Why you remained faithful but still received a frightening medical bill.
Why someone who barely acknowledges God seems financially comfortable while you, who pray and give, continue struggling.
Perhaps you stopped tithing because life became unbearable.
Perhaps you stopped because someone misused your generosity.
Or perhaps you've been giving faithfully for years, but deep inside, you're exhausted from wondering whether one missed tithe could somehow close heaven over your family.
If that is you, please don't leave this conversation yet.
Because the Bible has something much deeper to say about tithing than either “Give ten percent or God will punish you” or “Giving doesn't matter anymore.”
And somewhere between those two extremes stands Jesus Christ.
Not holding a calculator.
Not demanding that you purchase His affection.
But calling you into a relationship where grace transforms not only what you believe about money, but what money means to your heart.
And to understand that, we must go back to a verse that has comforted some believers, frightened others, and been misunderstood far too often.
“Will a man rob God?”
Those words come from Malachi 3:8.
They are serious words.
And we should never pretend otherwise.
God continues:
“Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings.” — Malachi 3:8, KJV
Then comes the verse that has caused generations of Christians to wonder whether financial hardship is evidence of divine displeasure.
“Ye are cursed with a curse: for ye have robbed me, even this whole nation.” — Malachi 3:9, KJV
Imagine hearing that when you're already barely surviving.
You are cursed.
Three words can become a prison when they are separated from their biblical context.
But before we apply those words directly to a struggling Christian today, we need to ask an essential question.
To whom was God speaking, and under what covenant?
Malachi was addressing Israel, a nation living under the covenant God established through Moses.
Under that covenant, tithes were not merely spontaneous donations to religious institutions. They were part of Israel's commanded system of worship, provision, and communal responsibility.
The Hebrew word translated “tithe” is מַעֲשֵׂר (maʿăśēr), meaning a tenth.
The Law connected tithes with the support of the Levites, who had no ordinary territorial inheritance like the other tribes, and with provision for vulnerable people.
Numbers 18:21 describes the Levites receiving tithes for their service.
Deuteronomy 14:28–29 describes a provision involving the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow.
This matters.
God's concern was never simply that money should move from ordinary people into religious hands.
His covenant instructions involved worship, justice, responsibility, and care for those who could not easily provide for themselves.
And when Israel neglected those obligations, it was not a harmless administrative mistake.
It was covenant unfaithfulness.
That is why Malachi's warning was severe.
But the passage also contains a remarkable invitation.

“Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.” — Malachi 3:10, KJV
The Hebrew expression אֲרֻבּוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם (ʾărubbōt haššāmayim) refers to the windows or floodgates of heaven.
It is a powerful picture of divine provision.
And in the agricultural setting of ancient Israel, God's promise was closely connected with the land, crops, and protection from destruction, as the following verse makes clear.
Malachi 3:11 speaks of God rebuking the devourer and protecting the fruit of the ground.
This was not originally a promise that every person who gives ten percent to a modern church will receive a larger bank balance.
It was a covenant promise addressed to Israel within a particular historical and theological setting.
That does not make the passage irrelevant to Christians.
It means we must understand it faithfully before applying its principles.
Because Scripture was not given so that we could take a sentence out of its setting and turn God into a financial transaction.
And this is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Some believers have been told that if they miss a tithe, God may withdraw His protection, damage their finances, or allow tragedy to enter their homes.
But Malachi 3 does not authorize us to declare that every Christian who fails to give ten percent is under a financial curse.
That is not a conclusion we can simply impose upon the New Testament.
And the reason is not that God has become less holy.
The reason is Jesus Christ.
Listen carefully to Galatians 3:13.
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.” — Galatians 3:13, KJV
The Greek word translated “redeemed” is ἐξηγόρασεν (exēgorasen), from a verb meaning to buy out or redeem.
Paul's point is not that Christians can now live selfishly without consequence.
His point is that Christ accomplished something no amount of human religious performance could accomplish.
He redeemed His people from the law's curse.
Think about that.
Jesus did not hang on the cross so that His followers would spend their lives terrified that a missed payment could reverse what His blood accomplished.
He did not cry, “It is finished,” only for our salvation to become dependent upon whether our giving records remain perfect.
And yet we must be precise.
Galatians 3:13 does not promise that Christians will never experience financial loss, suffering, discipline, or the consequences of unwise decisions.
It does mean that those who belong to Christ should not be taught that a missed ten-percent contribution automatically places them back under the Mosaic covenant's curse.
The cross is greater than that.
You cannot purchase the grace that Jesus already paid for with His blood.
But don't misunderstand this freedom.
Being free from the curse of the law is not the same as being free to worship money.
In fact, Jesus speaks about money with such seriousness that anyone using grace as an excuse for greed should feel deeply challenged.
“No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon.” — Matthew 6:24, KJV
The Greek word μαμωνᾶς (mamōnas) refers to wealth or possessions, especially as a rival master.
Jesus was not merely discussing how much money we give away.
He was exposing who rules our hearts.
Because money can become an idol whether you have millions or barely enough for tomorrow.
A wealthy person can cling to possessions.
A poor person can be consumed by the desire for possessions.
A church leader can turn financial giving into a measure of spiritual superiority.
And a wounded believer can become so suspicious of giving that generosity disappears entirely.
The question Jesus presses upon us is deeper than percentages.
Who owns your heart?
And that question reaches into places that an offering envelope never could.
Consider the rich young ruler in Mark 10.
He approached Jesus asking about eternal life.
He had religious knowledge. He had moral discipline. He had kept commandments from his youth, according to his own testimony.
Yet Jesus saw something beneath the surface.
Mark 10:21 tells us:
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him...”
Don't miss that.
Jesus loved him.
Before the young man surrendered his possessions.
Before he made a sacrifice.
Before he demonstrated the obedience Jesus was about to require.
Jesus loved him.
Then Jesus told him to sell what he had, give to the poor, and follow Him.
And the young man walked away sorrowful because he had great possessions.
The tragedy was not that he failed to complete a religious donation.
The tragedy was that when Jesus exposed the rival occupying his heart, he could not let it go.
Jesus loved him enough to confront what was enslaving him.
And sometimes, that is what God's Word does to us.
It comforts the frightened giver.
But it also confronts the comfortable hoarder.
It heals the person manipulated by religious fear.
But it also challenges the person who spends freely on personal pleasures while remaining indifferent to the needs of others.
Grace does not make generosity unnecessary.
Grace makes genuine generosity possible.
Now consider something extraordinary.
When the apostle Paul instructed New Testament believers about giving, he did not tell the Corinthian church that they must maintain a ten-percent payment to escape Malachi's curse.
Instead, he wrote:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
The Greek phrase μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης (mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs) means not out of grief or reluctance, and not out of compulsion or necessity.
And the word translated “cheerful” is ἱλαρόν (hilaron), describing a willing, glad disposition.
Paul is not saying giving should be careless or thoughtless.
He is describing generosity that arises from a heart moved by grace rather than controlled by pressure.
He also writes in 2 Corinthians 8:12:
Read that again.
According to what a person has. Not according to what a person does not have.
That sentence matters to the mother wondering how to feed her children.
It matters to the father searching for work.
It matters to the widow surviving on limited income.
It matters to the believer facing medical expenses, debt, or an unexpected financial emergency.
God does not need a religious performance that pretends you possess resources you do not have.
And when Paul discusses giving, he also emphasizes fairness, mutual care, and the relief of genuine needs.
In 2 Corinthians 8:13, he explicitly says that his purpose is not for others to be eased while the Corinthians are burdened.
That should make every Christian ministry examine the way it asks people for financial support.
A ministry should never use the fear of God's punishment to pressure struggling people into giving what they need for basic necessities.
And neither should believers use Paul's words to excuse a permanently closed hand when they genuinely have the ability to help.
Both truths belong together.
Now we need to address the question many people are still carrying.
If I stop tithing, will God stop blessing me?
The most biblically responsible answer is this:
The New Testament does not teach that Christians automatically lose God's blessing whenever they stop giving a fixed ten percent of their income.
Christians differ on whether the tithe remains a binding minimum under the new covenant.
Some regard ten percent as an enduring biblical standard for believers.
Others understand the Mosaic tithe as fulfilled within the old covenant and see New Testament giving as voluntary, proportionate, sacrificial, and guided by love.
Both perspectives should be examined seriously through Scripture.
But neither justifies treating God's grace as something people can buy.
Nor should we promise that every faithful giver will become financially prosperous.
Jesus Himself warned His disciples that they would experience trouble in this world.
Paul knew hunger, hardship, and need.
And faithful Christians throughout history have suffered poverty without being abandoned by God.
Financial comfort is not a reliable measurement of spiritual maturity.
Neither is financial hardship proof that God has withdrawn His love.
Sometimes financial difficulties arise from circumstances beyond our control.
Sometimes they result from poor decisions.
Sometimes generosity itself requires real sacrifice.
And sometimes we simply do not know why a season is so difficult.
What we must not do is pretend to know God's hidden judgment from someone's bank balance.
There is a difference between saying God cares about how we steward our resources and claiming that every financial crisis is punishment for insufficient giving.
The first is biblical.
The second can become spiritual cruelty.
And perhaps somebody reading this has carried that cruelty for years.
You lost a business.
You buried someone you loved.
You experienced an illness you never expected.
And somewhere along the way, someone suggested that perhaps you had not given enough.
So now you carry two burdens.
The suffering itself.
And the suspicion that God caused it because you disappointed Him financially.
Please hear this.
Your suffering is not evidence that Jesus has stopped loving you.
Look at the cross.
The most beloved and perfectly obedient Son suffered.
Not because He failed to give enough.
Not because He lacked faith.
But because He willingly entered suffering to accomplish our redemption.
The cross destroys the shallow assumption that suffering always proves divine displeasure.
And the resurrection declares that suffering does not have the final word.
But there is another side to this conversation that we cannot ignore.
Sometimes people stop giving not because they are struggling, but because their hearts have grown cold.
They still want God's protection.
They still want His comfort.
They still want His provision.
But they have become increasingly unwilling to participate in the work of His kingdom or help those in need.
Their resources are available for almost everything except generosity.
And they may need to hear a different question.
Not “Is God going to curse me?”
But “Lord, what has happened to my heart?”
Because there are forms of spiritual poverty that money cannot measure.
And there are people who possess very little yet demonstrate extraordinary generosity.
Remember the widow Jesus observed in Mark 12:41–44.
She placed two small coins into the treasury.
Jesus noticed.
He said that she had given more than those who contributed large amounts from their abundance, because she had given out of her poverty.
But notice the surrounding context.
Immediately before this account, Jesus warned against religious leaders who “devour widows' houses” (Mark 12:40).
That warning must not be ignored.
The widow's offering reveals the profound significance of sacrifice in Jesus' eyes. The passage also sits within a context that exposes religious exploitation.
It should never be used to demand that impoverished people surrender their last money to an institution while leaders ignore their needs.
Jesus saw the widow.
And He also condemned those who exploited the vulnerable.
Both truths matter.
Because the God who values sacrificial generosity also commands justice, mercy, and love.
And this brings us to a question that may be even more important than whether Christians are required to tithe.
What should giving look like when Jesus truly becomes Lord of our lives?
It should be willing.
It should be thoughtful.
It should be honest.
It should reflect our actual circumstances.
It should help sustain faithful ministry and meet genuine human needs.
It should be accompanied by integrity and accountability from those receiving the gifts.
And above all, it should point toward the grace of God rather than the glory of the giver.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 8:9:
Paul is speaking about the extraordinary self-giving grace of Christ, not guaranteeing that every Christian will become financially wealthy.
Jesus gave Himself.
Not ten percent of His mercy.
Not a carefully measured portion of His compassion.
He gave Himself.
And when that truth reaches the deepest places of our hearts, generosity begins to change.
We no longer ask only, “What is the minimum amount I must give so God will leave me blessed?”
We begin asking, “Lord, how can I honor You with what You have entrusted to me?”
For one believer, that may involve faithfully setting aside ten percent as a personal discipline.
For another, generosity may exceed that amount.

For someone in severe financial distress, faithful stewardship may involve caring for dependents, meeting essential obligations, receiving help from the church, and giving in ways appropriate to their actual capacity.
God sees the heart.
And He calls His people to both generosity and wisdom.
First Timothy 5:8 reminds believers of their responsibility to provide for their households.
First John 3:17 challenges those who possess material resources but close their hearts to a brother or sister in need.
These commands are not enemies.
They belong to the same life of love.
A mature Christian does not abandon family responsibilities in the name of generosity.
Nor does a mature Christian use family responsibilities as a permanent excuse for selfishness.
We are called to walk in wisdom, not extremes.
And if you've been wounded by financial manipulation in a church, please don't confuse the failures of people with the character of Jesus.
Some ministries have handled money dishonestly.
Some leaders have made promises Scripture never made.
Some have pressured people through fear, guilt, and exaggerated testimonies.
Those wrongs deserve accountability.
But the misuse of giving does not erase the beauty of genuine generosity.
There are faithful pastors serving quietly.
There are churches feeding hungry families.
There are ministries doing sincere work with limited resources.
And when Christians give freely to trustworthy, accountable Gospel work, their generosity can become part of something far larger than themselves.
Not because God needs our money to remain powerful.
But because He graciously allows His people to participate in His work.
That is an extraordinary privilege.
And it is the spirit in which I want to invite you to consider something personal.
At Gospel Warrior, our desire is to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through biblical teaching, discipleship, encouragement, and resources that help believers grow deeper in the Word.
Those resources are intended to help people who are hungry for Scripture, including those who may not be able to afford Christian books or study materials.
And work like this takes time, care, effort, and practical resources to continue and expand.
Not because God will love you more.
Not because your salvation depends on it.
But because freely supporting faithful Gospel work can be one meaningful way of honoring God with the resources He has entrusted to you.
Some believers may choose to include it within their personal giving budget or what they set aside for tithes and offerings.
It is voluntary support.
And that is precisely why it can be beautiful.
Because giving offered in freedom is different from money extracted through fear.
These products can become everyday reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to share your faith.
It is the opportunity to help make Scripture-centered encouragement and discipleship resources available to more people.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read, learn, grow, pray, and share the Gospel.
You can still access the free resources.
And you can still make a meaningful difference.
Perhaps it will reach a mother who has been giving out of terror rather than worship.
Perhaps it will reach a Christian who has become indifferent to generosity.
Perhaps it will reach someone who has never understood why Jesus went to the cross.
Not simply to increase the reach of a page.
But to put biblical truth where someone who needs it may encounter it.
Be honest about what is happening in your heart.
Have you been giving because you love God, or because you are afraid He will punish you?
Have you stopped giving because you genuinely cannot afford it, or because you no longer want to surrender control?
Have you been wounded by religious manipulation?
Or have you quietly allowed money to become the place where you seek security instead of trusting your heavenly Father?
You do not have to pretend.
You do not have to impress anyone.
And you do not have to disclose private financial details.
But perhaps today is the day you stop hiding the real struggle.
Because this conversation was never supposed to end with a percentage.
It was supposed to lead us back to a Person.
Jesus Christ.
The One who saw Zacchaeus, a man whose life had been marked by greed and dishonest gain.
The One who entered his home before Zacchaeus could repair all the damage he had done.
The One whose presence brought a transformation so real that Zacchaeus declared he would give half his possessions to the poor and restore fourfold what he had wrongfully taken.
Read Luke 19:1–10.
Jesus did not teach Zacchaeus how to purchase salvation through generosity.
He brought salvation into the house of a man whose encounter with grace produced repentance and restitution.
The money did not save Zacchaeus.
His changed relationship with money revealed something about the transformation taking place.
That is the Gospel.
Not money buying mercy.
But mercy transforming a life.
And maybe that is what you need today.
Not another frightening sermon about what will happen if you miss a payment.
Not another excuse to keep everything for yourself.
But a fresh encounter with the Savior who is both gracious enough to forgive and holy enough to transform.
If you have been afraid, bring that fear to Jesus.
If you have been selfish, confess it.
If you have been manipulated, seek truth and wise counsel.
If you have given with the wrong motives, ask Him to renew your heart.
If you have stopped trusting Him, begin again.
And if your finances are in ruins, remember that you are not disqualified from approaching the throne of grace.
Romans 8:32 asks:
“He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?”
That verse is not a blank check for luxury or an exemption from hardship.
It is an assurance rooted in God's greatest gift.
He has given His Son.
And because of Christ, those who belong to Him can trust that God's saving purpose and faithful care will not fail.
Perhaps you still have bills to pay tomorrow.
Perhaps your financial situation will not change overnight.
Perhaps you still need to make difficult decisions, seek employment, ask for help, reduce expenses, or rebuild after painful mistakes.
Faith does not eliminate those responsibilities.
But you can face them without believing that God's love is waiting on the other side of a transaction.
You can pray.
You can repent.
You can learn to give wisely.
You can receive help humbly.
You can grow in generosity.
And you can trust Jesus without pretending that every unanswered prayer is evidence of punishment.
So, does God withhold blessings when you stop tithing?
God is sovereign, and He takes the stewardship of our resources seriously. Scripture warns against greed, selfishness, and disobedience, and it teaches that generosity matters deeply.
But there is no New Testament basis for declaring that every Christian who fails to give ten percent automatically loses God's favor or comes under a financial curse.
God's blessing cannot be reduced to money.
His grace cannot be purchased through religious contributions.
And His love for His redeemed children does not rise and fall with the amount in an offering envelope.
That is not permission to stop being generous.
It is an invitation to become generous for a better reason.
Because you have encountered the generosity of Christ.
Because you have received mercy you could never earn.
Because you have discovered that everything you possess is ultimately entrusted to you by God.
And because you want your life, including your finances, to tell the truth about the Savior you follow.
One day, the money we worked so hard to accumulate will no longer matter in the way it does now.
The bills will be history.
The bank balances will be irrelevant.
The possessions we defended so fiercely will belong to someone else.
But what Christ has accomplished will remain.
And the love we demonstrated, the people we served, the needs we helped meet, and the faithfulness we practiced will have mattered in ways that cannot be measured by a bank statement.
So give when you can.
Give wisely.
Give willingly.
Support trustworthy Gospel work.
Care for your household.
Remember the poor.
Seek accountability.
And never mistake the size of your contribution for the size of God's love.
Because the greatest blessing God has ever given humanity did not arrive in an envelope filled with money.
It arrived in a manger.
It walked among sinners.
It touched lepers.
It welcomed the rejected.
It carried a cross.
And on the third day, the tomb was empty.
His name is Jesus.
And He is still changing hearts that money could never heal.
You may have nothing left to place in the offering envelope, but if you belong to Jesus, you have not lost the Savior who gave Himself for you.
